In the late starters, one of the favorites in Justin Rose is joined by Jordan Spieth and Brooks Koepka - shortly after his return from LIV Golf to the PGA Tour.

The tournament will get underway, as is the tradition, with the honorary starters on Thursday morning.

This year will see record six-time Masters winner Jack Nicklaus, 86, joined by three-time champion Gary Player, 90, and two-time winner Tom Watson, 76.

The field is 91 players , keeping with another Masters tradition. Augusta National prefers fewer than 100 players in the field, and it's been that way dating to 1967.

Scottie Scheffler plays out of a bunker during his practice round on Tuesday at Augusta

Tiger Woods will miss the Masters for the second straight year. He was arrested March 27 in Florida on a driving while intoxicated charge. No alcohol was found in his system, but drug experts determined he was impaired.

Woods entered a plea of not guilty last week, and then he issued a statement saying he was taking an indefinite leave to seek treatment.

His absence has been noted this week, although Jason Day questioned why he was behind the wheel of a car.

Phil Mickelson is not playing the Masters for only the third time as a pro. Mickelson says his family is navigating through a personal health matter. He already has missed four of five LIV Golf events because of the situation.

Hideki Matsuyama stopped for a selfie on the Hogan Bridge during a relaxed practice round

It's the first time since 1994 neither Mickelson nor Woods is at Augusta National. Back then, Woods was a senior in high school who had yet to become eligible. Mickelson broke a bone in his left leg skiing a few months before the Masters.

Thursday and Friday rounds start at 1 p.m. ET on Prime Video, the latest broadcast partner for Augusta National.

ESPN will take over at 3 p.m. on the weekday rounds through 7:30 p.m. Then on the weekend, Paramount+ will get started at noon, and CBS will carry live tournament coverage from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Sports.title: Kai Havertz strikes late as Arsenal steal victory vs Sporting Lisbon - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Kai Havertz strikes late as Arsenal steal victory vs Sporting Lisbon - 5 talking points

SPORTING LISBON 0-1 ARSENAL: Premier League leaders Arsenal stole a late victory against the Portuguese giants on Tuesday evening to see them put one foot in the Champions League last four

View 3 Images Kai Havertz celebrates his goal vs Sporting (Image: Getty Images)

Arsenal have one foot in the Champions League semi finals after Kai Havertz's late goal against Sporting Lisbon.

‌



After back-to-back defeats, Mikel Arteta's side once again struggled to find their fluency, having come up against a stubborn Sporting side.

‌



Martin Zubimendi thought he had given the Gunners the lead midway through the second period but had his goal ruled out for offside.

‌



Kai Havertz was the man to step forward in stoppage time to score what could be a vital win for the Gunners.

Here are all of the talking points from the José Alvalade Stadium:

Two Arsenal stars at risk of Champions League ban ahead of Sporting clash READ MORE :

Are Arsenal's Champions League opponents called Sporting Lisbon or Sporting CP READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Raya rescues Arsenal

Predictably, the home side started the game at a break-neck speed and could have been ahead but for some spectacular acrobatics from Arsenal stopper David Raya.

Maximiliano Araújo latched onto a brilliant pass from Diomande for Sporting and was faced with the Arsenal keeper one-on-one. He went for sheer power but Raya just about managed to get a fingertip to the ball and tip it onto the crossbar.

Raya also produced an excellent stop to parry away Geny Catamo's late header in what was an inspired performance.

‌



Gyokeres return falls flat

Don't get it wrong: Viktor Gyokeres is a hero in Lisbon. His record of 97 goals in 102 games for the Portuguese giants proves that.

While some were left disgruntled with the manner of his exit in the summer, they did not make that displeasure known, with any boos falling flat.

Unfortunately for Gyokeres, his return was equally as underwhelming. He really struggled to get involved throughout the evening and was even at fault for Arsenal's opener getting chalked off.

‌



View 3 Images Viktor Gyokeres had a difficult evening upon his return to Sporting Lisbon (Image: Getty Images)

Controversy denies Arsenal

Potentially the most frustrating element of Gyokeres' performance was his part in Arsenal's ruled out goal. The ball was played into the Swedish forward and he set it back.

Martin Zubimendi then curled home a divine right-footed strike. But the referee immediately intervened and cancelled the goal, which was the right decision.

‌



Gunners overcome frustration

Placed amid the backdrop of Arsenal's current stuttering form, there were reasons to be worried for Mikel Arteta. Arsenal lost the Carabao Cup final and have been eliminated from the FA Cup by a Championship side,

Arsenal of course have one target this season - the Premier League - but there's no getting away from the fact that it has been a damaging week.

View 3 Images Martin Zubimendi was rightfully denied a goal vs Sporting (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Havertz steals it

While a win would have been welcome, Sporting have not been slouches this season. The Portuguese giants have not lost on home soil in the Champions League this season and beat reigning champions PSG.

That was until Havertz stepped forward in the closing stages. He was expertly picked out and poked a clinical finish home.

It was arguably undeserved but not a single player in the Arsenal dressing room will care.

Sports.title: Rory McIlroy answers his own question as Masters champion targets new 'destination'
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy answers his own question as Masters champion targets new 'destination'

Rory McIlroy is loving every minute of being Masters champion as he prepares to defend his title at Augusta National, and he has the answer to a question he asked 12 months ago

View 3 Images Rory McIlroy is basking in the glow as reigning Masters champion at Augusta National (Image: Benjamin Gilbert/Augusta National/Getty Images)

Moments after slipping on the Green Jacket 12 months ago, Rory McIlroy turned the tables on reporters at Augusta National.

‌



“What are we going to talk about next year?” he asked, gleefully ready to leave behind nigh on 20 years of the same questions about how he would overcome the many heartaches he endured.

‌



Two days out from the opening round, McIlroy had the answer. With the career Grand Slam sewn up and sport’s most coveted coat resting proudly on his shoulders, the Ulsterman says he believes his legacy-defining 2025 win was not the “destination,” but a stop along the way.

‌



Drunk Masters fan arrested after repeatedly attempting to sneak in for free at Augusta READ MORE :

The 36-year-old is hungry for more glory. He said: “I think the story as it relates to me is what do I do from now onwards? What motivates me? What gets me going? What do I still want to achieve in the game? I think that's the story.

“And there's still a lot that I want to do. You think every time you achieve something or have success, you'll be happy, but then the goalposts move, and they just keep nudging a little bit further and further out of reach.

“I think what I've realised is, if you can just really find enjoyment in the journey, that's the big thing because, honestly, I felt like the career Grand Slam was my destination, and I got there, and then I realised it wasn't the destination.”

‌



For all the latest news and views from The Masters at Augusta National, visit The Mirror US.

View 3 Images McIlroy is eying more Masters glory (Image: Harry How/Getty Images)

McIlroy spent so much of his prime years feeling unfulfilled. A decade-long major drought, combined with inferior peers entering the pantheon of Green Jacket owners, stoked feelings of envy.

‌



Here, though, he exuded contentment. As the defence of his title neared, he cracked jokes and basked in the glow of being a reigning champion at Augusta, and the many perks that come with it.

The desire to burnish his CV with more major wins, coupled with a newfound patience and ease in himself, makes him a very dangerous prospect for his rivals.

“I think for the past 17 years, I just could not wait for the tournament to start, and this year I wouldn't care if the tournament never started. That's the difference,” he said.

‌



View 3 Images McIlroy was the first man on the course for a practice round on Tuesday (Image: Hector Vivas/Getty Images)

“It's completely different. I feel so much more relaxed. I know that I'm going to be coming back here for a lot of years, going to enjoy the perks that the champions get here.

“It doesn't make me any less motivated to go out there and play well and try to win the tournament, but yeah, just more relaxed about it all.”

‌



The pomp and ceremony, particularly Tuesday's champions’ dinner, have not distorted McIlroy’s priorities. He was first on the course in the Georgia morning dew on Tuesday, playing a full 18 holes.

McIlroy debuted at the Masters in 2009, and after waiting 17 excruciating years for the win he craved as a child, it is ironic that he sees this tournament as his best chance to add to his haul of five majors.

Masters pairings and start times confirmed as Rory McIlroy discovers playing partners READ MORE :

Jon Rahm's mixed emotions over who he sits by at Masters dinners READ MORE :

“I think when you've had the experiences that I've had around here, good and bad, I think that can stand to you,” he said.

Article continues below

“The other major venues, we don't go back to the same place every year. I'm still young, but I'm very experienced. I've been doing this for a long time.

“I do feel like I've got another 10 good shots at this. Not that I don't at the other majors, but I just think that everything here is a little more predictable. You know the golf course pretty much. I just think the more experience you have around this golf course, the better it is.”

Sports.title: Masters star needs security guards on every hole after traumatic health battle
Sports.content:
Masters star needs security guards on every hole after traumatic health battle

Gary Woodland arrives at Augusta National playing excellent golf, but under the surface, he is locked in a daily health battle, and he has opened up on the challenges he will face at Augusta National

View 2 Images Gary Woodland has bravely spoken about his battle with PTSD ahead of the Masters (Image: Benjamin Gilbert/Augusta National/Getty Images)

If you notice a few more security guards than usual following Gary Woodland at the Masters, there is a very good reason.

‌



The 2019 US Open champion is battling post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after having a brain tumour removed in 2023, and he has bravely opened up on the challenges he faces on and off the course.

‌



Woodland wrote one of sport's great comeback stories two weeks ago when he won the Texas Children's Houston Open on the PGA Tour to secure an invitation to the Masters. In the face of such adversity, the 41-year-old is playing some of the best golf of his life.

‌



Drunk Masters fan arrested after repeatedly attempting to sneak in for free at Augusta READ MORE :

As he closed in on his emotional victory in Houston, his opponent was his mind rather than the other players in the field. Woodland experiences hypervigilance and can be deeply unsettled by unexpected movement around him.

To his enormous credit, he was able to overcome his anxieties on the course and ploughed on to claim his first victory since his US Open triumph at Pebble Beach seven years ago.

Augusta National runs a tight ship, and instances of patrons becoming unruly are rare, but Woodland says seeing the presence of security staff helps calm his mind.

‌



For all the latest news and views from The Masters at Augusta National, visit The Mirror US.

View 2 Images Woodland blew away the field to win the Houston Open two weeks ago (Image: Getty Images)

"Just like on tour, I'll have security with me," he said. "The main deal is they were showing me where security is. The whole deal for me is it's visual, right? If I can see somebody, then I can remind myself that I'm safe constantly.

‌



"So I have a good idea now where security is on every hole. The big deal for me, my caddie knows too. So he can constantly remind me.

"Like I said, I don't have control when this thing hits me, and it's tough. It can be a fan. It can be a walking score. It can be a camera guy running by me, just any startlement from behind me can trigger this pretty quickly. Knowing where the security is is a constant reminder that I'm safe."

Woodland bravely revealed his PTSD diagnosis in March, just two weeks before his win in Houston. Although the victory was deeply satisfying, he remains locked in a daily mental battle.

Article continues below

Jon Rahm's mixed emotions over who he sits by at Masters dinners READ MORE :

Masters pairings and start times confirmed as Rory McIlroy discovers playing partners READ MORE :

"I know what I'm battling every day. People ask me, 'How was the win?' The one thing I know is that having this brain tumor and having PTSD, it doesn't matter if I win or lose. It doesn't care," he said. "I had a tough time last week battling this stuff. A lot of stimulation comes with winning, stuff I hadn't seen in a long time.

"It's a big week for me this week. The fans are very close on the tee boxes. There's a lot going on. There's probably not a safer golf tournament in the world, so I'm happy for that, but it's still a battle in my head if I'm safe or not. That's a tough pill to swallow.

"I'm emotional from the standpoint that I know how close I probably was to never being back here, and I'm very proud of myself for earning my way back."

Sports.title: Rory McIlroy's nine-word response to Masters Dinner question he's constantly been asked
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy's nine-word response to Masters Dinner question he's constantly been asked

Rory McIlroy has issued a response to a Masters Dinner question after the 2025 champion picked his choices for guests ahead of this year's tournament

View 2 Images Rory McIlroy ahead of this year's Masters in Augusta (Image: Getty Images)

Rory McIlroy has joked he 'didn't go more Irish' with his Masters Dinner because he wants to "enjoy" the meal as well. McIlroy, 36, won the famous green jacket for the first time in 2025 and has been able to pick what is on the menu for his first-ever Masters Champion Dinner at Augusta National.

‌



For appetizers, McIlroy has given players a peach and ricotta flatbread, rock shrimp tempura, bacon wrapped dates and grilled elk sliders to chose from. As for the starter, there is yellowfin tuna carpaccio with a main course of either wagyu filet mignon or seared salmon. There is just one dessert offer on the menu in the form of a sticky toffee pudding with vanilla ice cream and warm toffee sauce.

‌



Guests will have that with champagne and a selection of high-end wines. And McIlroy's dinner is said to be valued as the most-expensive ever at £251 per head, three times more expensive than Scottie Scheffler's menu last year.

‌



Jon Rahm's mixed emotions over who he sits by at Masters dinners READ MORE :

Masters pairings and start times confirmed as Rory McIlroy discovers playing partners READ MORE :

Despite this, McIlroy has been asked why he hasn't included more Irish-based foods and choices on his menu. The five-time major champion was born in Holywood, County Down, in Northern Ireland.

Joking about that, McIlroy said in a press conference on Tuesday: "People keep asking me, 'Why didn't you go more Irish?' And I say, 'Because I want to enjoy the dinner as well.'"

McIlroy also said he was encouraged to have one vegetarian option, which is why he included the peach and ricotta flatbread. "I think that one was probably for Gary Player," he added.

‌



View 2 Images Rory McIlroy speaking as Masters winner (Image: Getty Images)

Although McIlroy is defending Masters champion, he comes into the tournament as the joint-third favourite at 12/1 behind Scheffler (11/2), Jon Rahm (10/1) and alongside Bryson DeChambeau (12/1) and Xander Schauffele (12/1).

When quizzed about coming into the 2026 Masters as defending the iconic green jacket, McIlroy said: "For the past 17 years, I could not wait for the tournament to start. This year, I couldn’t care if the tournament never started... Doesn’t make me any less motivated to try to win, but just more relaxed about it all."

Article continues below

Reflecting on his win last year, McIlroy added: "It feels absolutely incredible. Can't believe it was 12 months ago that I was sitting here and trying to take it all in.

"To be able to come back and do this press conference in a green jacket, that feels pretty good. It's been an amazing 12 months taking this thing around the world."

Sports.title: Drunk Masters fan arrested after repeatedly attempting to sneak in for free at Augusta
Sports.content:
Drunk Masters fan arrested after repeatedly attempting to sneak in for free at Augusta

Augusta is the place to be this week as Rory McIlroy bids to defend his Masters title, but tickets for the golf major are expensive and difficult to get hold of

View 2 Images An "intoxicated" golf fan has been arrested for trying to get into Augusta without their own ticket (Image: 2025 Getty Images)

An intoxicated golf fan has been arrested for trying to sneak into Augusta for the Masters. Tickets for the iconic golf major are few, far between and expensive.

‌



This week, it will be one of the most exclusive events in the USA, with only 40,000-50,000 patrons allowed to be in attendance each day. A four day tournament badge is understood to cost around $525 (£396 approximately), but tickets are being sold on re-sale sights for five-figure sums.

‌



Millions of golf fans have to enter a lottery system in a bid to earn a ticket for the major, but few are lucky enough to get one. One golf fan, Matthew Stroud, has been formally charged with trespassing after sneaking into Augusta.

‌



Jon Rahm's mixed emotions over who he sits by at Masters dinners READ MORE :

Masters pairings and start times confirmed as Rory McIlroy discovers playing partners READ MORE :

The Richmond County Sheriff’s Department spotted Stroud asking for the ticket badges of spectators as they left the North Gate of Augusta at the end of Monday's practice round. His efforts to obtain a ticket were soon picked up by Augusta security personnel and local officers, who told him to leave the area.

Stroud, who was also described as being "intoxicated" by officers, returned to the area in a desperate bid to get hold of a badge. Unsurprisingly, he was, once again, told to leave the area.

But after refusing to depart the vicinity, police on the scene arrested him for criminal trespassing and took him to the Charles B. Webster Detention Centre, where he was formally charged with trespassing.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

He was eventually released by officers after he paid a bail bond of $285 (£215). Stroud is one of millions of golf fans who have missed out on getting a ticket for the event.

Series badges, which grant access to all three days as well as the practice events, are even more difficult to get hold off. Stroud will instead have to watch the event, which starts on Thursday, on the television.

‌



He and many other golf fans will now be able to look up the tee times of their favourite players. Rory McIlroy will be with Cameron Young and Mason Howell for the first two rounds.

View 2 Images The golf fan was reportedly arrested at the North Gate entrance of Augusta (Image: Augusta National Archives)

The Northern Irishman's title defence will see him tee off at 10:31am local time and 3:31pm BST on Thursday. World No. 1 Scottie Scheffler will play alongside Robert MacIntyre and fellow US star Gary Woodland and will be the penultimate group to tee off, starting at 1.44pm local time and 6.44pm BST.

Article continues below

Before the competition began, McIlroy made it clear he will do everything he can to become the fourth player to defend the Masters after Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods and Nick Faldo.

He said: "I know defending the Masters tournament is a pretty rare feat. It's something I'd love to do. I've won it once and I feel like that will make it a bit easier for me to win again."

Sports.title: Jake Paul responds to claims he called off engagement to Winter Olympics hero Jutta Leerdam
Sports.content:
Jake Paul responds to claims he called off engagement to Winter Olympics hero Jutta Leerdam

YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul has broken his silence amid bombshell claims he has called off his engagement to his fiancee Jutta Leerdam

View 2 Images Jutta Leerdam and Jake Paul (Image: (Melina Pizano/Getty Images for Netflix))

Jake Paul has denied claims he has called off his engagement to his fiancee Jutta Leerdam. The YouTuber-turned-boxer has issued a statement in which he takes aim at the 'false information' which has emerged online over the course of the last week.

‌



Dutch media personality Yvonne Coldeweijer first shared the rumours of their split. She said: "Jutta has been dumped by her fiancé Jake! He is completely done with her!

‌



"Two weeks ago Jake dropped her off at home, took the ring from her, and broke off the engagement and thus the relationship."

‌



Coldeweijer's claims also alleged that Paul had cheated on his speed-skater fiancée in recent weeks. However, there is no evidence to support her allegations.

But responding to the speculation, Paul took to X and wrote: "Seeing the Dutch media lying about my fiancé Jutta and I. There is so much false information being spread about Jutta in the past years. It needs to stop."

Dutch speed skater Leerdam finally capped her long career by taking gold in the women's 1000 metres long-track speed skating final at the Winter Olympics earlier this year. She also won silver in the women's 500m event.

After winning gold, Leerdam paid tribute to Paul and her family, who she said had provided support that she had struggled to reciprocate.

She said: "I've been supportive, but I've not been able to go to his [Paul's] past fights because of skating. It would be nice to be there more.

"He has supported me a lot more and has come to many of my races, so I'm very grateful. Also, my family - I'm just so grateful for the support system around me. It's amazing."
